name: Battle of Austerlitz
info: Napoleon's Grande Armée defeated a combined Russian and Austrian army near Austerlitz in Moravia on 2 December 1805, in the War of the Third Coalition, and Austria then left the war by the Treaty of Pressburg.

facts.place: About ten kilometres south-east of Brno, between Brno and Austerlitz (Slavkov u Brna), then in the Austrian Empire, now in the Czech Republic
facts.sides: The French Empire's Grande Armée under Napoleon I, some 72,000 men and 157 guns on one account; the Allied army under Tsar Alexander I and General Kutuzov with Austrian forces under Emperor Francis II, about 85,000 men and 318 guns on the same account
facts.outcome: The French broke the Allied centre and routed the Allied army, taking thousands of prisoners. France and Austria agreed a truce on 4 December and signed the Treaty of Pressburg on 26 December.

t: Napoleon pretended to be weak, gave up the Pratzen Heights and thinned his right flank, so that the Allies weakened their own centre to attack it; Soult's corps then took the Heights.
Davout's III Corps marched 110 km in 48 hours from Vienna to hold the French right against a much larger force.
Figures differ: one account gives the Allied army as 85,000 and the French as 72,000, another 89,000 and 66,000, and the Allied losses are given as about 36,000 against about 9,000 French.
dyk: Napoleon's letter to Joséphine spoke of a victory over the army commanded by 'the two emperors', which gave the battle its name of the Battle of the Three Emperors, though Emperor Francis of Austria was not present on the field.
ev: 200,000 French troops begin to cross the Rhine on a front of 260 km
Vienna falls, and Napoleon sets a trap by seeming weak and abandoning the Pratzen Heights
The Allied council adopts Weyrother’s plan, and Napoleon hides his troops behind the Bosenitz stream
The French take the Pratzen Heights and break the Allied centre, and the Allied army abandons the field
France and Austria sign a truce on 4 December
The Treaty of Pressburg takes Austria out of the war on 26 December

sections.background:
Europe had been in turmoil since the French Revolutionary Wars began in 1792. In 1797 the French Republic broke up the First Coalition, and a Second Coalition formed in 1798 was defeated by 1801, leaving Britain the only opponent of the French Consulate. Britain and France agreed to end hostilities in the Treaty of Amiens in March 1802, but problems persisted. The British resented returning captured colonies, Napoleon was angry that the British refused to abandon Malta, and the situation worsened when he sent an expeditionary force to Saint-Domingue. In May 1803 Britain declared war on France.

In December 1804 an Anglo-Swedish agreement led to the Third Coalition. By April 1805 Britain and Russia had signed an alliance, and Austria, defeated twice in recent memory and keen on revenge, joined a few months later. In August Napoleon, Emperor of the French since December 1804, turned from the English Channel to the Rhine. On 20 October 23,000 Austrians surrendered at Ulm, bringing the Austrian prisoners of the campaign to 60,000, and Vienna fell in November.

Napoleon's long lines of communication and the unknown intentions of Prussia left him needing a battle. Kutuzov planned to retreat further, towards the Carpathian region. Napoleon set a trap: he gave the impression that his army was weak and wanted peace, and on 27 November ordered Soult to abandon Austerlitz and the Pratzen Heights in apparent disorder. Many Allied officers, including the Austrian chief of staff Franz von Weyrother, urged an immediate attack, and Kutuzov's plan was rejected.
sections.forces:
The core of the Grande Armée had been the force assembled at Boulogne for a planned invasion of Britain, and it was organised in seven corps, each with 36 to 40 cannon and able to act alone until others came to its aid. By 1805 it had grown to 350,000 men. At Austerlitz Napoleon had some 72,000 men and 157 guns, with about 7,000 under Davout still far to the south. The Allies had about 85,000, seventy per cent of them Russian, and 318 guns. Another figure gives the armies as 89,000 and 66,000.

The Russian army had no permanent formation above the regiment, its senior officers were mostly aristocrats and its junior officers often undertrained, but its soldiers were steadfast and its artillery fine. The Austrian army had begun reforms under Archduke Charles, who lost influence when Austria went to war against his advice; Karl Mack instituted further changes. Its cavalry was good but often outnumbered, and its artillery was the best in the Coalition but no better than the French.

The Allies adopted Weyrother's plan: a main drive on the French right, which looked lightly guarded, with diversions against the French left, in four columns. The Russian Imperial Guard was held in reserve and Bagration guarded the Allied right. The Tsar took the command from Kutuzov and gave it to Weyrother. Napoleon weakened his right on purpose and hid his main force in dead ground. Davout was to hold the Goldbach first with 5,000 and then 12,500 men against Buxhoeveden's 43,000, while Soult's 16,000 struck the centre.
sections.course:
The battle began at about 8 a.m. with Allied attacks on Telnitz, held by the 3rd Line Regiment. Heavy fighting drove the French out, the first men of Davout's corps arrived and threw the Allies out, and artillery checked further attacks. The Allied columns came on more slowly than intended. Liechtenstein's cavalry, moved from the left to the right, slowed part of the second column. Sokolnitz, defended by the 26th Light Regiment and skirmishers, changed hands several times.

Meanwhile Kutuzov's IV Corps stopped on the Pratzen Heights, but the Tsar ordered it to withdraw. At about 8:45 a.m. the mist was clearing and Napoleon saw the weakness of the Allied centre. Soult said his men needed less than twenty minutes to reach the Heights, and about fifteen minutes later Napoleon ordered the attack with the words 'One sharp blow and the war is over.' St. Hilaire's division was forced back by delayed Allied detachments and Austrians, then struck again and cleared the Heights. Vandamme's division broke several Allied battalions at the Old Vineyards.

Grand Duke Constantine's Russian Imperial Guard counterattacked and defeated a battalion of the 4th Line Regiment, the only French standard lost. Napoleon sent in his own Guard cavalry, and Drouet's division then deployed on the flank. The Russians broke, and Kutuzov was severely wounded. Lannes drove Bagration off the field in the north. St. Hilaire and part of Davout's corps then broke through at Sokolnitz, and the Allied army abandoned the field in all directions.
sections.aftermath:
Allied casualties are given as about 36,000 out of 89,000, about 38 per cent of their effective forces, and French losses at around 9,000 out of 66,000, about 13 per cent. The Allies also lost 186 guns and 45 standards. In one retreat, a famous but disputed episode, Russian troops under Dokhturov withdrew over the frozen Satschan ponds, where French artillery fire broke the ice. Estimates of the guns captured range from as few as 38 to more than 100, and of the dead from 200 to 2,000. Local evidence made public later suggests Napoleon's account was exaggerated: when the lakes were drained days later only two or three bodies and some 150 horses were found.

France and Austria signed a truce on 4 December, and the Treaty of Pressburg followed on 26 December. Austria recognised the French gains of the treaties of Campo Formio and Lunéville, ceded land to Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden, paid 40 million francs and ceded Venice to the Kingdom of Italy. The Russian army was allowed to withdraw home. Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine, and Francis dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. Prussia went to war with France in 1806. Napoleon gave two million francs to his higher officers and 200 francs to each soldier, with pensions for the widows of the fallen.
sections.sources:
Accounts of the battle disagree on its numbers. One gives the armies at the start as about 72,000 French and 85,000 Allies, another as 66,000 and 89,000, and a third puts the French near 53,000 before reinforcements. Allied casualties are given as about 36,000 and French as around 9,000, and for the Satschan ponds the estimates of the dead range from 200 to 2,000 and of the guns captured from as few as 38 to more than 100.

Much of what is told of the battle comes from Napoleon. His letter to Joséphine called it a victory over the army 'commanded by the two emperors', though Francis was not on the field. His proclamation claimed that a Russian army of seventy-six thousand men had been annihilated, a figure that fits none of these strengths. His account of the ponds is thought exaggerated: when the lakes were drained a few days after the battle, the bodies of only two or three men were found, with some 150 horses, although Tsar Alexander attested to the incident after the wars. Russian data confirm heavy losses at the ponds without giving a number.

Other matters are later tradition or dispute. The saying 'Never interrupt your enemy when he is making a mistake' derives from a story first recorded by Archibald Alison in 1836 and is called apocryphal. Blame for the Allied defeat was assigned differently: it has been placed on Alexander I and Weyrother for accepting a battlefield of Napoleon's choosing, while the Tsar himself blamed Kutuzov afterwards.
sections.legacy:
Austerlitz is often cited by military historians as one of Napoleon's tactical masterpieces, in the same league as Cannae and Gaugamela, and it was the decisive engagement of the War of the Third Coalition. It did not bring a lasting peace: it drove neither Russia nor Britain to settle, and Prussian worries about French influence led to the War of the Fourth Coalition in 1806. Some historians suggest Napoleon was so successful that he lost touch with reality, and that French foreign policy became a personal one after the battle. He did not defeat the Allied army as thoroughly as he wanted. It has also been argued that Kutuzov's plan to retreat further might have let the Allies be reinforced by Archduke Charles's troops and the Prussians join the Coalition.

In France the battle was revered in the 19th century by authors such as Victor Hugo. Napoleon never awarded a victory title for it. Government bonds rose from 45 to 66 per cent of face value on the news. At the bicentennial in 2005 neither President Chirac nor Prime Minister de Villepin attended commemorations, and some residents of France's overseas departments protested against what they saw as the official commemoration of Napoleon.

Tolstoy made the battle the close of the first volume of War and Peace. The Colonne Vendôme in Paris was first called the Column of Austerlitz, and the Pont and Gare d'Austerlitz carry its name. Since 1992 the battlefield has been a protected landscape monument zone, with the Cairn of Peace Memorial, built in 1910 to 1912 and dedicated in 1923, near Prace.

summary: At Austerlitz on 2 December 1805 Napoleon's army broke the centre of a larger Russian and Austrian army after luring it off the Pratzen Heights. Austria left the war within weeks by the Treaty of Pressburg, but Russia and Britain did not settle.

notes: Strength figures conflict inside the article: 72,000 French and 85,000 Allies in the Battle section, 66,000 and 89,000 in the results section, 53,000 and 89,000 (75,000 with reinforcements) in the preliminary moves. I gave the first two pairs and left the third out.

The article gives Francis II as commanding the Austrian army but says he was not present on the field; the info line names him as leader only of the Austrian side and the facts line puts him with the Allied command, which the editor may prefer to reword.
The article says Kutuzov arrived at the battlefield on 9 September 1805, which cannot be right for a campaign that began in August and September; I left it out.

The article blames Alexander I and Weyrother for the trap and says the Tsar blamed Kutuzov; both are given. It also says the Tsar's withdrawal of IV Corps 'pushed the Allied army into its grave': I left that wording out.
Buxhoeveden 'completely drunk' is an unsourced claim in the article; it is mentioned only as unsourced in the sources section and could be removed.
Napoleon's proclamation says a Russian army of 76,000 was 'annihilated'; I mention the figure only as his claim.
The date of the truce is 4 December, but the article also says the armistice was signed at Slavkov Castle on 6 December; I used 4 December and left 6 December out.
Casualty figures for Allies and French come from one passage; no attribution is given in the article.

Left out for length: Napoleon's letter to Talleyrand about Joséphine, Pitt's 'Roll up that map', Alexander's 'babies in the hands of a giant', the list of 19 municipalities, the Hoffmann/Jadin note, the monuments near Utrecht.
